title: The gods' council: Enkidu must die
ref: Gilg. SB VII (from the Hittite version)
short: Enkidu dreams that the gods meet and decide that one of the two friends must die for killing Humbaba and the Bull.
body: Thompson's text has only the opening question; George fills the gap from a Hittite version (already used in translation by Friedrich and Ungnad, as Thompson's note says). Anu, Enlil, Ea and Shamash debate; Enlil insists that Enkidu, not Gilgamish, must die, and Shamash's protest is overruled. The death of the friend in place of the hero is the epic's central tragedy.

title: Enkidu's curse on the courtesan
short: Dying, Enkidu curses the trapper and the courtesan for bringing him out of the wild; Shamash rebukes him.
body: In George's fuller text the curse is long and elaborate, consigning the woman to a life on the streets. Shamash reminds Enkidu of what civilisation gave him (bread, beer, clothing, a friend) and of the honours he will have in death. Enkidu relents and pronounces a blessing. The episode asks whether human life is worth the price of mortality and civilised knowledge.

title: Shamash's rebuke
short: Shamash reminds Enkidu that the woman gave him food 'for divinity', drink 'for royalty' and Gilgamish as friend.
body: The speech lists the gifts of humanisation from Tablet II. It also promises Enkidu a hero's funeral: a great couch, homage from the princes of the underworld, the lament of Uruk. Gilgamish will repeat these words in Tablet VIII. Shamash's argument is that a short human life is still worth living for its goods and its bonds. In George's text Enkidu is calmed and his 'angry heart grew quiet'.

title: 'Hades': Thompson's word for the underworld
short: Thompson's 'Hades' renders Akkadian ersetu, 'the earth', the usual word for the underworld.
body: Thompson's own note offers 'of the earth' as an alternative. The Mesopotamian underworld is literally 'the earth', below ground; using the Greek 'Hades' gives a classical colour but imports Greek associations. In Tablet XII the refrain 'only the earth hath seized him' depends on this word. Thompson's choice is consistent: 'Hades' recurs in the dream of the underworld, where 'the Recorder of Hades' renders the title of the underworld scribe. Students reading Greek epic alongside Gilgamesh should not infer any historical link from the word itself; the Mesopotamian 'Land of No Return' has its own conventions.

title: Mourning in a lion skin
short: Shamash foretells that Gilgamish will let his hair grow, wear a lion's skin and roam the wild in mourning.
body: Neglect of the body was a sign of mourning; the lion skin makes Gilgamish a wild man like the early Enkidu. The image has long been compared with Heracles' lion skin; the possibility of Near Eastern influence on the Heracles myth is debated among scholars. The prophecy is fulfilled in Tablets VIII-X, where Gilgamish roams the wild in skins. The image of a hero in a lion skin who travels to the ends of the earth inevitably recalls Heracles, but the link is debated and the motif may simply be a common image of the wild man.

title: Enkidu's blessing on the courtesan
short: Enkidu blesses the woman: kings and princes will love her and give her gifts.
body: Thompson's 'Mayst thou be left as the mother of seven brides' renders a broken line which in George's text says that for her sake a wife, 'mother of seven', will be abandoned, i.e. that men will leave their wives for her. The blessing reverses the curse point by point. Shamash's rebuke has persuaded Enkidu to reverse his curse, so the courtesan ends as a figure of honour. The episode shows the poem's balanced view of the civilising woman: she brought him to death, but also to friendship and a human life.

title: Enkidu's dream of the death-messenger
short: Enkidu dreams of a dark-faced man with lion's (or eagle's) claws who seizes him and leads him to the underworld.
body: Thompson's note asks whether this is the harbinger of death who carries Enkidu off. In George's text the figure has the face of the Anzu-bird and talons of an eagle; he turns Enkidu's arms into feathered wings. This is the most detailed vision of the Mesopotamian underworld outside the Descent of Ishtar. The vision combines elements of Mesopotamian demonology, in which death-demons with lion or bird features drag victims below. Enkidu is turned into a bird-like creature, matching the dead who wear feathers. The dream is a direct premonition of his death.

title: The House of Dust
short: The underworld is a house of darkness from which no one returns, where the dead eat dust and wear feathers like birds.
body: Thompson's note calls Irkalla the presiding deity of the underworld; it is also a name of the underworld itself. These lines appear almost word for word in the Descent of Ishtar, showing a shared poetic formula. The dead there include former kings, priests, the legendary Etana and the god Shakkan, all equal in the dust: a bleak vision that drives Gilgamish's search for life.

title: Etana
short: Etana was a legendary king of Kish who flew to heaven on an eagle's back to find the plant of birth.
body: Thompson's note: 'The hero of a legend, who was carried up to heaven on an eagle.' Even he, who sought a plant of life (for a son), sits in the dust; the parallel with Gilgamish's plant (XI) is suggestive. Etana appears in the Sumerian King List among the earliest kings. The Etana legend is one of the oldest Akkadian narratives, known in Old Babylonian and later versions; Dalley translates it. Its presence among the dead is a reminder that even the great kings of legend share the fate of all men. The mention also prepares Tablet XI, where Gilgamish finds and loses a plant of youth.

title: Ereshkigal, Queen of the Underworld
short: Ereshkigal ('Lady of the Great Earth') is queen of the dead, sister of Ishtar.
body: Thompson's note: her name 'has made its way into an ancient Greek charm' (she is invoked as Ereschigal in Greek magical texts). Her scribe, Belet-seri, reads the records of the dead before her. Ereshkigal appears in Tablet XII as 'the mother of Ninazu'. In the myth of Nergal and Ereshkigal she marries the god Nergal, who becomes king of the underworld. In the Descent of Ishtar she is the sister and adversary of Ishtar. She is the ultimate authority over the dead, and the scribe reading before her suggests a judgement of the newcomer.

title: Belet-seri, scribe of the underworld
short: Belet-seri ('Lady of the Steppe') is the scribe of the underworld who reads the tablets before Ereshkigal.
body: The bureaucratic underworld reflects Mesopotamian society, where scribes kept records. Her looking up at Enkidu suggests his name is now on the list of the dead. Thompson's 'Recorder of Hades' renders her function, and the name itself is restored in his text. Belet-seri was also a goddess of the steppe, the open land where Enkidu was born, so the figure who records his arrival among the dead has a link with his origins. George discusses her role in the commentary on Tablet VII.
